Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 52
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: School Principal
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 58

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.

Vignette:
Daniel, a 52-year-old married school principal, had always considered himself the kind of man who could walk into any room and quickly take stock of it. That habit took on a different meaning after the night he was assaulted outside a parking lot near his school. He had stayed late for an evening event, locked up the building, and was crossing toward his car when he was confronted and attacked. What stayed with him afterward was not a clear narrative he could easily call up at will, but fragments that arrived uninvited: the hard sense of his body pinned in place, the shock of being unable to move the way he wanted, and the brutal immediacy of the moment when he understood he was not safe. When he later tried to describe it, he found that deliberately reaching for the memory was oddly difficult, as if the details were just out of grasp. Yet when the memory came on its own, it did not feel distant or past. It played through his mind like a film he had never consented to watch, with the same sequence of movements and the same surge of helplessness, so vivid that he would sometimes go still in the middle of a conversation.

In the months that followed, Daniel became someone who noticed danger before anything else. He would enter the school auditorium, the grocery store, the dentist’s waiting room, or a restaurant with his wife and immediately scan for exits, registering doors, hallways, and the easiest way out. He did this almost without thinking, but he was aware of how quickly his eyes moved and how little comfort he took from settling into a seat. He also found himself noticing objects he had never paid attention to before—potential weapons, hard edges, things that could be used to hurt someone. In a classroom, he would catch sight of a heavy trophy, a metal flagpole, a broken chair leg, and feel his attention lock onto it for a moment longer than seemed reasonable. At home, even ordinary items on a counter could pull his gaze because his mind seemed to catalogue what might be dangerous before he could redirect it.

These changes were especially hard to hide at work, where his role required him to appear calm and available to students, parents, and staff. As principal, he moved through hallways, offices, and assembly spaces every day, and each building he entered offered fresh opportunities for the same quick, silent survey of exits and objects. He noticed himself lingering near doorways and feeling a jolt when someone approached from behind unexpectedly in the corridor. A student dropping a book or a chair scraping abruptly across the floor could make him jump in a way that embarrassed him. He tried to smooth over these moments with a professional smile, but afterward he would feel unsettled and overly alert, as though his body had not gotten the message that the danger was over. At home, his wife began to notice that he paused longer than usual before entering unfamiliar spaces and that he seemed less relaxed when they went out together. He remained committed to his routines, but there was less ease in them, and he often caught himself choosing where to sit based on sightlines rather than comfort.

The memory intruded in ways that were both frustrating and physically unsettling. When a thought, sound, or sudden movement brought it back, Daniel did not merely remember the assault; he seemed to re-enter a body position that matched the event. His shoulders tightened, his chest felt fixed, and he had the distinct sensation of being held in the same posture he had been in that night. He could sense how his body had been arranged by force, and that physical echo made the memory harder to dismiss as something that had happened long ago. He was not inclined to talk about it much, in part because he had trouble pulling together the details in a straightforward account and in part because when he did try, the images arrived in that repetitive, film-like way that left him drained and irritated with himself. He had come to believe that there was something undignified about how much the memory still affected him, especially given his responsibilities as a school leader who was supposed to project steadiness.

Over time, Daniel’s vigilance and the replaying memory shaped the way he moved through daily life. He became more deliberate about where he stood in rooms and more alert to who was behind him. He did not describe himself as paranoid, but he knew he was on guard in a way that tired him out. What finally brought him to seek help was the growing strain of keeping this contained while continuing to function as the public face of a school. He was most afraid that he would remain caught in this state of jumpiness and intrusive replay, forever pulled back into the same body memory whenever he least expected it. At the same time, he hoped for something simpler and more practical: to walk into a room without immediately searching for ways out, to sit through a meeting without tracking every object that could be turned into a weapon, and to feel his own body settle again when the memory came to mind.
